1. Core meaning  
   • The person elected or appointed to preside over a meeting, committee, board of directors, or organization.  
   • In many companies the chairman (or chairperson) leads the board and oversees corporate governance, while day-to-day operations are run by the Chief Executive Officer (CEO).

2. Typical responsibilities  
   • Set the agenda for board meetings and keep discussion on track.  
   • Ensure all directors receive accurate, timely information.  
   • Facilitate balanced participation and decision-making.  
   • Act as liaison between the board and senior management.  
   • Oversee evaluation of the CEO and senior executives.  
   • Uphold corporate governance standards and stakeholder interests.  
   • Represent the organization externally when appropriate.

3. Position in organizational structure  
   • Chair of the Board (often non-executive) → Oversees governance and strategy.  
   • CEO (executive) → Runs the company’s day-to-day business.  
   • In some smaller organizations one person holds both roles; in others they are deliberately separated to avoid concentration of power.

4. Variants and inclusive language  
   • Chair, chairperson, board chair, presiding officer – gender-neutral alternatives increasingly preferred in policy documents and bylaws.  
   • “Madam Chair” or “Mister Chair” are accepted forms of address in formal meetings.

5. Related terms  
   • Vice-chair (deputy who steps in when the chair is absent).  
   • Presiding officer (generic term used in parliamentary procedure).  
   • President (in some nonprofits and academic bodies, this title can be equivalent to chair).

6. Example sentence  
   “The chairman called the meeting to order at 9 a.m. and guided the directors through the quarterly agenda.”

7. Usage tip  
   When drafting contemporary policies, use “chair” or “chairperson” unless the organization’s bylaws explicitly specify “chairman.”', refusal=None, role='assistant', audio=None, function_call=None, tool_calls=None, annotations=[]))], created=1755575908, model='openai/o3-high', object='chat.completion', service_tier='default', system_fingerprint=None, usage=CompletionUsage(completion_tokens=685, prompt_tokens=528, total_tokens=1213, completion_tokens_details=CompletionTokensDetails(accepted_prediction_tokens=0, audio_tokens=0, reasoning_tokens=256, rejected_prediction_tokens=0), prompt_tokens_details=PromptTokensDetails(audio_tokens=0, cached_tokens=0)))

1. Definition  
   Epidemiology is the study of the distribution (who, when, where) and determinants (causes, risk factors, protective factors) of health-related states or events in specified populations, and the application of this study to the control of health problems.

2. Core concepts  
• Population focus: Looks at groups, not individuals.  
• Disease frequency: Measured mainly through incidence (new cases) and prevalence (existing cases).  
• Comparison: Identifies associations by comparing groups—exposed vs. unexposed, treated vs. untreated, etc.  
• Causation vs. correlation: Uses structured criteria (e.g., Bradford Hill) and study designs to infer causal relationships.  
• Prevention & control: Converts findings into policy, guidelines, and interventions.

3. Key measures  
• Incidence proportion (risk) = new cases / population at risk over a period.  
• Incidence rate = new cases / person-time at risk.  
• Prevalence = all cases / total population at a point (point prevalence) or over a period (period prevalence).  
• Mortality rate, case-fatality rate, years of potential life lost (YPLL), disability-adjusted life years (DALYs), etc.  
• Association metrics: risk ratio (RR), odds ratio (OR), rate ratio, risk difference, population attributable fraction (PAF).

4. Main study designs  
Observational  
 • Cross-sectional: snapshot of exposure and outcome.  
 • Ecological: aggregates (countries, counties).  
 • Cohort: follows exposed vs. unexposed over time.  
 • Case-control: starts with cases, looks backward for exposures.  
Experimental  
 • Randomized controlled trial (RCT): investigators allocate exposure.  
 • Community trials, pragmatic trials.

5. Bias & confounding  
• Selection bias, information (measurement) bias, recall bias, loss to follow-up.  
• Confounding: extra variable related to both exposure and outcome.  
• Methods to handle: randomization, restriction, matching, stratification, multivariable regression, instrumental variables.

6. Modern extensions  
• Molecular and genetic epidemiology (gene–environment interactions).  
• Pharmacoepidemiology (drug safety & effectiveness).  
• Social epidemiology (socioeconomic, behavioral determinants).  
• Spatial epidemiology and GIS mapping.  
• Infectious-disease modeling (R0, epidemic curves, agent-based models).  
• Data science & digital epidemiology (mobile data, social media for surveillance).

7. Applications  
• Outbreak investigation (e.g., tracing a food-borne illness).  
• Noncommunicable disease control (cardiovascular risk, cancer screening).  
• Environmental & occupational health (air pollution, asbestos).  
• Health services evaluation (effectiveness, equity).  
• Policy development (vaccination schedules, smoke-free legislation).

8. The epidemiologic process (field investigation example)  
1. Verify diagnosis & confirm outbreak.  
2. Define case & count cases.  
3. Describe by time, place, person.  
4. Develop hypotheses.  
5. Test hypotheses (analytic studies).  
6. Implement control measures.  
7. Communicate findings.

9. Essential skills and tools  
• Biostatistics, study design, database management.  
• Critical appraisal of literature (systematic reviews, meta-analyses).  
• Ethical considerations (informed consent, data privacy).  
• Collaboration: clinicians, laboratorians, social scientists, policymakers.

10. Classic achievements  
• John Snow and the Broad Street pump (cholera, 1854).  
• Framingham Heart Study (cardiovascular risk factors).  
• Doll & Hill’s studies linking smoking to lung cancer.  
• Smallpox eradication, polio near-eradication.  
• HIV epidemiology shaping prevention strategies.

In short, epidemiology provides the evidence base for public-health action, transforming data on “who gets sick and why” into strategies that prevent disease, prolong life, and promote health at the population level.', refusal=None, role='assistant', audio=None, function_call=None, tool_calls=None, annotations=[]))], created=1755575908, model='openai/o3-high', object='chat.completion', service_tier='default', system_fingerprint=None, usage=CompletionUsage(completion_tokens=1065, prompt_tokens=530, total_tokens=1595, completion_tokens_details=CompletionTokensDetails(accepted_prediction_tokens=0, audio_tokens=0, reasoning_tokens=192, rejected_prediction_tokens=0), prompt_tokens_details=PromptTokensDetails(audio_tokens=0, cached_tokens=0)))
